hero.headline.text: From "help me learn" to an executable task

hero.highlight.text: Write the task as a contract that can be checked independently

hero.takeaway.text: The program finishing and the executor saying "done" do not mean the task is complete. Completion is decided by a validator that compares the task card against the tool evidence.

concepts.01-goal.description.text: "Help me learn about agents" has no scope, no deliverable, and no end point, so nobody can tell whether it is done. This lesson shrinks the task to 19 + 23, and every condition can be written out.

concepts.02-check.title.text: The task card comes before the run

concepts.02-check.description.text: Before execution, the task card writes down the goal, input scope, deliverable, evidence, failure handling, and stop condition. The validator goes by this card and nothing else.

concepts.03-evidence.title.text: Finished is not the same as passed

concepts.03-evidence.description.text: The flow reaching the report stage only shows that Python did not raise an error. With missing evidence or a wrong result, the acceptance check still fails.

concepts.04-claim.title.text: A claim must be checked against evidence

concepts.04-claim.description.text: When the executor says "the answer is 42", that is only a completion claim. The validator follows evidence_ref in the claim to this run's tool_result and looks at what the value actually is.

section-1.title.text: From "help me learn" to an executable task

section-1.paragraphs.0.text: The program finishing and the executor saying "done" do not mean the task is complete; completion has to be checked against criteria written in advance and against actual evidence. {{lesson:fail-safely}} left a question open: the run ended as completed and the model gave an answer, but did the task actually get done? In that lesson only you could judge, by reading the answer. This lesson hands the judgment to a program. It does not call a model; every step runs in local Python. With the flow fixed, you can see exactly how the judgment is made.

section-1.paragraphs.1.text: In its chapter on evaluation, *Understanding AI Agents in Depth* (深入理解 AI Agent) records a real failure. An agent operating a phone had to enter the expenses shown in an image into a bookkeeping app. It took more than thirty steps, none of them raised an error, and in the end it declared itself done. A later check found that the records it should have written did not exist. The few expenses it entered were invented, because it could not see the image at all. Looking only at whether the run raised an error, or at what the agent says about itself, cannot catch a failure like this.

section-1.paragraphs.2.text: To be checkable, the task itself must first be stated clearly. The sentence "help me learn about agents" lacks three things: which materials to use, what to deliver, and when it counts as done. Without them, no answer can be reviewed. This lesson shrinks the task to the minimum: "answer 19 + 23 based on a local computation". The input is two integers, the deliverable is one number, the evidence is the result of one computation tool call, and every condition can be written out.

section-1.paragraphs.3.text: A real task has to answer the same questions first: who supplies the facts, which operations are allowed, and what needs a human's confirmation. For example, when asking a coding agent such as Cursor or Claude Code to "fix the login failure", a checkable way to write it is: which directories may be changed, which group of tests must go from failing to passing, tests that passed before must not turn red, and when it cannot fix it, it stops and explains where it is stuck.

section-2.title.text: The task card writes down the acceptance rules

section-2.paragraphs.0.text: Before execution, the task card writes the acceptance criteria as six fields; the executor works to it and the validator checks against it. The six fields of TASK_CARD are: goal states the goal, "依据本地计算结果回答 19 + 23" ("answer 19 + 23 from the local computation result"); input_scope limits the data that may be used, only 19 and 23, with no external files or web pages; output states what is delivered, the value 42, noting that it comes from this run's computation; evidence states which evidence to look at and what condition it must meet, that the computation tool returned successfully and the result equals 42; failure states how to report when the conditions are not met, clearly marked as not passed; stop states when to stop, after one computation and one acceptance check.

section-2.paragraphs.1.text: Each of the six fields guards against one kind of problem. Without input_scope, the executor might search the web for an answer; without evidence, the acceptance check could only look at the wording of the answer; without failure, a failure might be written up as "mostly done"; without stop, the executor might keep adding calls. The conditions written down must be checkable by a program: "the result equals 42" works, "the answer is clear and easy to understand" does not, and the latter has to be turned into something that can be checked.

section-2.paragraphs.2.text: The task card must be written before execution. If you run first and then write the standard while looking at the result, the standard will drift toward the result without your noticing. At the start of a run, runtime.py publishes the task card as a lesson.task_card event, and whatever the executor hands in afterward, the acceptance check is made only against this card. Changing the task card changes what is being checked; making the answer sound more confident does not change the check result.

deep-dive-benchmarks.summary.text: Public agent benchmarks also fix the success criteria first, then check against facts a machine can verify.

deep-dive-benchmarks.paragraphs.0.text: In its chapter on evaluation, *Understanding AI Agents in Depth* breaks down a task from the telecom domain of τ²-bench. The ticket given to the agent says: the user's phone cannot get online, the user will not change plans but is willing to top up data if needed, and the problem counts as solved only if the speed test reaches the top tier. The simulator playing the user has its own instructions: do not admit the problem is solved unless the speed test reaches the top tier, and answer questions about device state strictly from tool results. Before the evaluation, both sides are reset to the same starting state; after the run, assertions check the actual state: whether mobile data works, and whether the speed test reached the top tier. All these conditions are fixed before the run, and nothing the agent says can change them.

deep-dive-benchmarks.paragraphs.1.text: Code-repair evaluations go a step further and split "fixed" into two independent claims. SWE-bench Verified uses two groups of tests: one group fails before the fix and passes after, proving the problem was really solved; the other passes both before and after, proving nothing else was broken. Check only the first group and the agent can delete an inconvenient assertion to get through; check only the second and you have checked nothing.

deep-dive-benchmarks.paragraphs.2.text: These two examples have the same structure as this lesson's task card: the goal, scope, evidence, and rules of judgment are all fixed before execution; the judgment looks only at facts a machine can verify, such as the speed test result, whether tests pass, and the values tools return, not at the executor's own statements. The only difference is scale: this lesson has one rule and one number, while a benchmark has hundreds or thousands of tasks.

deep-dive-benchmarks.paragraphs.3.text: As for the phone bookkeeping example at the start, the book also analyzes its root cause: the agent could read only the text structure of the interface and never received the image's pixels. The problem was not that the model cannot read images, but that the harness gave it no channel to see the image. A failure like this is exposed only by checking against external facts; the agent's own report shows nothing unusual.

predict-missing-evidence.prompt.text: Before you run "Fault injection: no tool call, just claim 42", predict: how many tool_result events will this run have?

mq-card-evidence.evidence-field.prompt.text: The task card's evidence says "计算工具成功返回且结果等于 42" ("the computation tool returned successfully and the result equals 42"). What does this field do?

mq-card-evidence.evidence-field.a.text.text: It fixes the evidence to check in advance, so the acceptance check does not depend on the wording of the answer

mq-card-evidence.evidence-field.a.feedba.text: Correct. The rules are set before the run, so the conclusion can be reviewed.

mq-card-evidence.evidence-field.b.text.text: It prompts the model to write a more confident answer

mq-card-evidence.evidence-field.b.feedba.text: Not quite. However confident the wording, it does not change the check result.

mq-card-evidence.evidence-field.c.text.text: It replaces the computation tool and gives 42 directly

mq-card-evidence.evidence-field.c.feedba.text: Not quite. It only specifies which evidence is needed; the evidence still has to be actually produced by the tool.

mq-card-evidence.evidence-field.explanat.text: The acceptance criteria are written in the task card, and the validator compares them with the actual result.

section-3.title.text: The run ending and the acceptance check passing are two different things

section-3.paragraphs.0.text: "Done" has at least three meanings, to be judged separately: the flow ended, the tool executed successfully, and the task passed acceptance. Whether the flow ended is read from the terminal state, and every scenario in this lesson ends as completed; whether the tool executed successfully is read from the ok of tool_result; whether the acceptance check passed depends on whether all the conditions on the task card are met. The first being true does not imply the last.

section-3.paragraphs.1.text: The report from verify states this relationship directly. Its first item, "执行过程已结束" ("the execution has ended"), is true in every scenario; it only says that Python reached the acceptance step. The conclusion is decided by the four items after it: whether the claim cites this run's tool evidence, whether the tool returned successfully, whether the value in the evidence is 42, and whether the claim and the evidence agree. accepted skips the first item and looks only at whether the last four all pass.

section-3.paragraphs.2.text: Take the "Claim only, no evidence" arm. The flow ends as usual and the first item is true; the executor claims the answer is 42, and that answer is right. But the second item, "声明引用了本次的工具证据" ("the claim cites this run's tool evidence"), is false, the items after it are false too, and the conclusion is not passed. A right answer by chance does not mean the task was completed as required: the task card asks for an answer based on a local computation, and without a computation record that cannot be shown.

section-4.title.text: One rule covers both normal and failure cases

section-4.paragraphs.0.text: All the presets share the same piece of acceptance code; only the evidence changes. "Normal" computes 19 + 23; "Claim only, no evidence" calls no tool and directly claims the answer is 42; "Evidence present, wrong result" computes 19 + 22 and honestly reports 41; "Claim and evidence disagree" computes 19 + 22 but claims 42. Apart from "Normal", these errors are all faults deliberately injected by the runner, not mistakes made by a model; this lesson has no model at all.

section-4.paragraphs.1.text: Why not write a separate judgment for each case? Because the acceptance rules must be fixed before the evidence. If you see the evidence is wrong and then change the rules to let it pass, the rules have lost their meaning. With fixed input, fixed rules, and only the evidence swapped, you can see clearly how the validator judges at each boundary; when a real model is connected later, the same rules still work. It is the same idea as writing tests: normal and edge cases run the same assertions.

mq-fault-injection.wrong-result-meaning..text: The wrong_result preset gets 41 from 19 + 22. What does this show?
It is a teaching fault injection, showing how the same acceptance rules handle a wrong result
Correct. The input was changed deliberately by the program; the rules did not change.
The model got the addition wrong
Not quite. This lesson does not call a model; the error is injected by the preset.
Not quite. Python computed 19 + 22 correctly; it just does not satisfy the task card.
Fixed input lets you see how the validator handles edge cases.

section-claim.paragraphs.0.text: A completion claim is only a statement the executor hands in; its job is to point to where the evidence is, not to serve as evidence. You can require an agent to hand in a completion claim when it finishes, for example {status: done, answer: 42, evidence_ref: task_add_1}. This lesson's executor is a fixed script in the runner that hands in the claim in place of an agent. evidence_ref in the claim points to the id of a tool call in this run.

section-claim.paragraphs.1.text: When the validator gets a claim, it does not reach a conclusion from the claim's answer; it follows evidence_ref to find the matching tool result in the evidence recorded this run, then compares the value in the evidence against the task card and against the claim in turn. The claim in the "Claim only, no evidence" arm has no evidence_ref, so the validator has nowhere to look and can only judge it not passed.

section-claim.paragraphs.2.text: The "Claim and evidence disagree" arm is more subtle: the tool actually returned 41, but the executor wrote 42 in the claim and attached the evidence_ref of this very call. An acceptance check that reads only the claim would pass it; only by following the reference to the tool_result do you find that the two do not match. When discussing validators, *Understanding AI Agents in Depth* puts it bluntly: an agent can easily write a report saying the task is fully done when in fact it is not.

section-claim.paragraphs.3.text: So the validator keeps two rules: use the claim only to locate evidence, never to reach a conclusion; and the evidence must come from the record made during execution, not rewritten by the executor afterward. This lesson's evidence is the return value of context.call_tool, and the same result is also recorded as a tool_result event, so you can compare them; this lesson does not demonstrate evidence being tampered with.

deep-dive-independent.title.text: Why the validator must be independent of the executor

deep-dive-independent.summary.text: Letting the executor judge itself just swaps the acceptance check for yet another claim.

deep-dive-independent.paragraphs.0.text: The laziest acceptance check is to ask the executor: "Are you done?" The trouble is that when the executor judges itself, it uses the same information and the same blind spots as when it executed. In the phone bookkeeping example earlier, that agent wrote "I can't see the expenses in the image" in its own mid-run reasoning, yet kept going and in the end declared itself done anyway. Ask it to check itself and it will just say "done" again.

deep-dive-independent.paragraphs.1.text: Independence has two layers. The first is independence of information: the validator reads only the task card and the evidence recorded during execution, not the executor's description of the process. The second is independence of rules: the rules of judgment are written as code and fixed before execution, so the executor cannot influence them. This lesson's verify satisfies both: its inputs are only the claim and the evidence, and all five checks are fixed comparisons.

deep-dive-independent.paragraphs.2.text: The reverse also happens: the work was done right, but the final statement was wrong. The book cites a public baseline result from τ²-bench: runs that required informing the user failed 240 times, and in 80 of them the environment state was correct and only the information given to the user was wrong, one third of all failures. So acceptance has to check both the evidence and whether the claim agrees with it. This lesson's fifth item, "声明与证据一致" ("the claim agrees with the evidence"), does exactly that: when the tool computed 41 and the claim says 42, it is false.

deep-dive-independent.paragraphs.3.text: Claude Code's official best practices say the same thing. The docs say Claude stops when the work looks done; without a check it can run itself, "looks done" is the only signal. So the docs recommend giving it a check that returns pass or fail, such as the exit code of tests or a build, and having it show evidence: the test output, the command it ran, and what it returned, not just a claim of success. To turn the check into a hard gate, you can configure a Stop hook: each time it is about to finish, it runs your check script, blocks if it fails, and hands the reason back so it keeps fixing; the docs also set a cap on consecutive blocks. You can also start a separate reviewer with a clean context and show it only the changes and the standard, so the one doing the work does not grade itself. The former corresponds to independence of rules, the latter to independence of information.

deep-dive-independent.paragraphs.4.text: Writing rules as code has another benefit: the same input gets the same verdict every time, so it can be run repeatedly and reviewed. Some standards cannot be written as code, such as whether an explanation is clear; the common approach is to ask another model to review it, but that is a judgment with uncertainty, which itself needs to be tested, and later lessons cover it. This lesson does only the part that can be written as code.

misconception-claim.claim.text: If the program ends normally and the agent says "done", the task is complete.

misconception-claim.correction.text: The terminal state completed only says the flow ran through, and a completion claim is only the executor's statement; neither is evidence. Whether the task is complete is decided by the validator checking the tool results recorded this run against the task card written in advance: missing evidence, a wrong value, or a claim that does not match the evidence all count as not passed.

mq-claim.claim-mismatch-reason.prompt.text: In the claim_mismatch scenario, the executor claims the answer is 42 and cites the record of this run's add_numbers call. Why does the validator judge it not passed?

mq-claim.claim-mismatch-reason.a.text.text: The cited tool_result holds 41, so the claim and the evidence do not match

mq-claim.claim-mismatch-reason.a.feedbac.text: Correct. The validator reads the evidence; the 42 in the claim is only a statement.

mq-claim.claim-mismatch-reason.b.feedbac.text: Not quite. It cites a real call from this run; the problem is in the cited content.

mq-claim.claim-mismatch-reason.c.text.text: The tool was called only once, which is not enough

mq-claim.claim-mismatch-reason.c.feedbac.text: Not quite. The number of tool calls is not a check item on the task card.

mq-claim.claim-mismatch-reason.explanati.text: The claim is used only to locate evidence; the conclusion is decided by the evidence and the task card.

section-5.title.text: The report traces back to actual evidence

section-5.paragraphs.0.text: The passed of every check in lesson.report can be traced back to this run's tool_call and tool_result. The report's table puts each attempt's "声明的答案" (claimed answer), "证据中的值" (value in the evidence), "验收结论" (acceptance verdict), and the reason for not passing in one row. Take a value from the table, find the matching tool_result on the timeline, and you should be able to derive the verdict exactly.

section-5.paragraphs.1.text: The validator checks only what the task card wrote down. In this lesson evidence says "计算工具成功返回且结果等于 42" ("the computation tool returned successfully and the result equals 42"), so verify only looks at whether the tool succeeded and whether the result is 42, not whether the tool computed 19 and 23. If the executor computed 20 + 22, the result would be 42 all the same, and these checks would pass it, even though it violates input_scope. To close this gap, you would add "the arguments are 19 and 23" to evidence and have the validator check the call's arguments. What the task card leaves out, the validator will not fill in for you.

section-5.paragraphs.2.text: The lab bench's "Executor's completion claim" is written only into the claim's summary; writing "all done" there will not change any of the checks. Open-ended tasks need more cases and external facts to be checked; this lesson shows only the skeleton of acceptance.

mq-what-verify-checks.what-verify-checks.text: Suppose the executor computed 20 + 22, the tool returned 42, and the claim also says 42 and cites this call correctly. How would this lesson's validator judge it?
Passed: evidence only requires the tool to succeed and the result to equal 42
Correct. The validator checks only the conditions the task card wrote as check items, and does not check the call's arguments.
The task card does write input_scope, but verify does not check arguments, so this one is not blocked.
Not passed: the claim and evidence disagree
Not quite. The claim says 42 and the evidence is also 42; they agree.
What the task card leaves out, the validator will not fill in for you; to check arguments, write them into evidence and add a check item.

section-goal-loop.title.text: Preview: the goal loop with a limit

section-goal-loop.paragraphs.0.text: When the acceptance check fails, you can hand the reason back to the executor and let it try again; this is the goal loop. Its structure is: execute, validate independently, retry with the reason if not passed, and stop on a pass or at the limit. The preset "Goal loop with a limit" demonstrates exactly this structure: attempt 1 has an error injected and the validator writes down the reason; attempt 2 redoes it according to the task card and stops after passing, leaving the remaining attempts unused.

section-goal-loop.paragraphs.1.text: The limit has to be written into the task card's stop field; the goal_loop scenario rewrites it as "验收通过或尝试 N 次后停止" ("stop on acceptance or after N attempts"). Without a limit, a task that can never pass acceptance would retry forever. Claude Cookbooks has an example of a loop that alternates generating and reviewing; it says this kind of loop fits when there are clear criteria for judging. The example itself uses a loop with no cap, so as long as the reviewer never passes the work, it keeps running. If you set this lesson's limit to 1, the loop stops after the first failure and honestly reports "达到尝试上限" ("attempt limit reached"), and the verdict is still not passed. Whether to stop is decided by the limit; whether it passed is decided by the evidence.

section-goal-loop.paragraphs.2.text: This lesson's executor is a fixed script that does not read the reason the validator wrote, and the correction in attempt 2 is written in advance. Whether a real model corrects it properly after reading the reason has to be tested with real runs, and {{lesson:goal-loops}} implements the full goal loop. Before that, {{lesson:structured-output}} deals with another problem: if what is to be delivered is itself a piece of JSON written by the model, how do you check it?

walkthrough.description.text: Step by step, this explains the structure of the validator; the code is a simplified illustration. This run's evidence is in the events on the lab bench.

walkthrough.step-1.title.text: Validate the input first, then publish the task card

walkthrough.step-1.body.text: INPUT_MODEL validates the scenario and the attempt limit; the task card is published as lesson.task_card before execution.

walkthrough.step-2.title.text: Call the tool and leave evidence

walkthrough.step-2.body.text: add_numbers is really executed in Python, and the platform records the call and the result as a pair of events.

walkthrough.step-3.body.text: The claim holds the answer and evidence_ref. It is only a statement and has not been checked yet.

walkthrough.step-4.title.text: Follow the reference to read the evidence

walkthrough.step-4.body.text: verify uses evidence_ref to find the tool_result, and compares the value in the evidence against the task card and the claim.

walkthrough.step-4.evidence.text: The passed and detail of each item in the report

walkthrough.step-5.title.text: Stop on a pass; if not passed, check the limit

walkthrough.step-5.body.text: In the goal loop, if not passed and the limit is not reached, try again and record the reason in lesson.goal_check; in other cases, stop and report the reason.

code-acceptance.n21.text.text: The task card puts the goal, input scope, deliverable, evidence, failure handling, and stop condition into six fields; it is published as lesson.task_card when the run starts.

code-acceptance.n25.text.text: evidence states a checkable condition: which tool succeeded and what the result equals. The check items that follow judge against it one by one.

code-acceptance.n36.text.text: The validator's inputs are only the completion claim and the evidence recorded this run; it ignores how the executor describes the process.

code-acceptance.n39.text.text: It finds evidence only by following the evidence_ref in the claim. If the claim cites the id of some other call, what you get here is empty.

code-acceptance.n44.text.text: The first item is always true: the flow reaching here only shows that Python did not raise an error.

code-acceptance.n48.text.text: Compare the value in the evidence against the task card; in wrong_result the evidence exists and the tool succeeded, but it stops at this item.

code-acceptance.n51.text.text: The claim and the evidence are compared on their own: claim_mismatch is blocked right here.

code-acceptance.n58.text.text: accepted skips the first item. The flow finishing and the task passing are two different things.

code-attempt.n61.text.text: The executor is a fixed script that hands in the completion claim in place of an agent. The faults are injected by the runner and are not mistakes made by a model.

code-attempt.n65.text.text: missing_evidence hands in a claim without calling the tool: the answer happens to be right, but there is no evidence to check.

code-attempt.n67.text.text: An injected fault changes only the evidence, not the acceptance rules. goal_loop makes only attempt 1 go wrong.

code-attempt.n71.text.text: The tool result is stored in evidence by call id, and the validator trusts only the record here.

code-attempt.n73.text.text: The executor in claim_mismatch reports 42 no matter what the tool returns, simulating a claim that reports only good news.

code-goal-loop.n81.text.text: The number of attempts is decided by max_attempts; other scenarios are fixed at 1 attempt, so each fault stays visible on its own.

code-goal-loop.n83.text.text: The goal loop writes the limit into the task card's stop field; the stop condition is also part of the contract.

code-goal-loop.n87.text.text: A goal loop with a limit: each attempt is "execute → independent acceptance check", at most limit times.

code-goal-loop.n93.text.text: Each attempt goes to the same validator; the executor's claim cannot change the check rules.

code-goal-loop.n98.text.text: Every attempt publishes lesson.goal_check: whether it passed, the reason if not, and whether the next step is retry or stop.

code-goal-loop.n104.text.text: Stop on a pass. Without this line, the loop would use up the remaining attempts.

code-goal-loop.n107.text.text: The report is assembled in _report: the check items, the metrics, and the record of each attempt.

code-decision.title.text: Acceptance is computed from evidence by an independent check, trusting neither the claim nor the run status

code-decision.chosen.text: Every passed in lesson.report is derived from this run's tool_result. The executor's claim is used only to locate evidence; neither the answer in the claim nor whether the run ended takes part in the verdict.

code-decision.status-as-success.title.text: Treat the run's terminal state completed as task success

code-decision.status-as-success.why_not.text: The missing_evidence scenario also runs to the end, so the status alone cannot tell "finished" from "done correctly".

code-decision.self-report.title.text: Trust the answer in the executor's claim

code-decision.self-report.why_not.text: The claim in claim_mismatch says 42 while the evidence is 41. Checking a claim with the claim is the same as not checking at all.

acceptance.title.text: One task card, three kinds of evidence

acceptance.hypothesis.text: The acceptance verdict is decided only by the evidence the task card specifies: when tool evidence is missing or the result is not 42, it cannot pass, even if the flow ended normally and the executor claims to be done.

acceptance.missing-evidence.label.text: Fault injection: no tool call, just claim 42

acceptance.card-evidence.text.text: The task card's evidence: it states before execution what evidence is needed.

acceptance.card-failure.text.text: The task card's failure: when evidence is missing or the value does not match, it must be marked as not passed.

acceptance.tool-evidence.text.text: The actual return value of add_numbers: 42 in the normal arm, 41 in the wrong-result arm; the missing-evidence arm has no such event.

acceptance.ended-check.text.text: The report's first item, "执行过程已结束" ("the execution has ended"): true in all three arms.

acceptance.value-check.text.text: The report's fourth item, "证据中的值满足任务卡" ("the value in the evidence meets the task card"): the expected value is shown next to the value in the evidence.

acceptance.claim-verdict.text.text: The report table: the claimed answer, the value in the evidence, and the acceptance verdict in one row.

acceptance.guide.0.text.text: This lesson does not call a model; the whole flow is run by local Python. First look at the task card published when the run starts.

acceptance.guide.1.text.text: The acceptance criteria were fixed before execution: there must be a successful computation result, and it must equal 42.

acceptance.guide.2.text.text: The failure rule is also written up front: missing evidence or a mismatched value must be clearly marked as not passed.

acceptance.guide.3.text.text: This is the only tool evidence in this run. If you ran the missing-evidence arm, this will say there is no such evidence in this run, which is exactly the situation that arm is meant to show.

acceptance.guide.4.text.text: The first check is true in all three arms: the flow reached the acceptance step, but that does not mean the task succeeded.

acceptance.guide.5.text.text: This item puts the expectation next to the value in the evidence, and the verdict follows from them.

acceptance.guide.6.text.text: The missing-evidence arm's claimed answer is also 42, yet the verdict is not passed: whether the answer is right is a matter for the evidence, not for the claim.

acceptance.conclusion.proves.0.text: This run's acceptance verdict can be traced item by item to the task card's rules and the actual values in tool_result.

acceptance.conclusion.proves.1.text: "执行过程已结束" ("the execution has ended") is true in all three arms, yet the verdicts differ: the run ending does not mean the task passed.

acceptance.conclusion.does_not_prove.0.text: Missing evidence and a wrong result are faults injected by the runner, not real mistakes made by a model.

acceptance.conclusion.does_not_prove.1.text: A task card that checks only 19 + 23 cannot prove that open-ended tasks can be accepted this way; real tasks also need more cases and external facts.

claim-vs-proof.title.text: The claim says 42, the evidence says 41

claim-vs-proof.hypothesis.text: As long as the validator follows evidence_ref to read the evidence, a claim with the right answer in it cannot fool it; a validator that reads only the claim will be fooled.

claim-vs-proof.mismatch.label.text: Fault injection: the evidence is 41, the claim says 42

claim-vs-proof.claimed-answer.text.text: The answer the executor claims: both arms write 42.

claim-vs-proof.claim-ref.text.text: The evidence_ref in the claim: both arms point to this run's real add_numbers call.

claim-vs-proof.referenced-value.text.text: The value in the cited tool_result: 42 in one arm, 41 in the other.

claim-vs-proof.consistency-check.text.text: The report's fifth item, "声明与证据一致" ("the claim agrees with the evidence"): the only item that catches claim_mismatch.

claim-vs-proof.guide.0.text.text: The claims in the two arms look exactly the same. Look at the claim itself first.

claim-vs-proof.guide.1.text.text: The answer is 42 in both. If the validator read only this, both arms would pass.

claim-vs-proof.guide.2.text.text: The claim also carries evidence_ref. The validator uses it to find the matching tool result.

claim-vs-proof.guide.3.text.text: The value in the evidence is what was actually computed this time. When you run claim_mismatch, this is 41.

claim-vs-proof.guide.4.text.text: When the claim and the evidence agree, this item is true; when they do not match, it is false and the overall acceptance check fails.

claim-vs-proof.conclusion.proves.0.text: Two claims that both say 42 get different verdicts, and the difference comes only from the cited tool_result.

claim-vs-proof.conclusion.proves.1.text: Every check of the validator reads the evidence recorded this run; the answer in the claim takes no part in the verdict.

claim-vs-proof.conclusion.does_not_prove.text: The claim in claim_mismatch is built by the runner and does not mean any model would do this; a real model's completion claims have to be tested with real runs in later lessons.
evidence_ref can be checked only on the premise that the platform records the evidence and the executor cannot change it; this lesson does not demonstrate evidence being tampered with.

goal-loop.title.text: Preview: the goal loop with a limit

goal-loop.hypothesis.text: When acceptance fails, record the reason and try again; stop on a pass. With a limit of 1, the loop stops after the first failure and honestly reports not passed.

goal-loop.three-attempts.label.text: Limit 3: attempt 1 gets an injected error, attempt 2 redoes it

goal-loop.loop-stop.text.text: The task card's stop field: the limit is written into the contract.

goal-loop.first-reasons.text.text: The reason attempt 1 failed acceptance: the value in the evidence is not 42.

goal-loop.first-next.text.text: The decision after attempt 1: retry with a limit of 3, stop with a limit of 1.

goal-loop.second-pass.text.text: The acceptance result of attempt 2: the loop ends once it passes.

goal-loop.stop-reason.text.text: The stop reason in the report: acceptance passed, or the attempt limit was reached.

goal-loop.guide.0.text.text: This arm only previews the structure of the goal loop; the correction in attempt 2 is a fixed script, with no model involved.

goal-loop.guide.1.text.text: First look at the stop condition: stop on a pass, or after attempts reach the limit.

goal-loop.guide.2.text.text: Attempt 1 had an error injected, and the validator wrote down the reason it did not pass.

goal-loop.guide.3.text.text: The next step is decided by the limit: retry if attempts remain, stop if not.

goal-loop.guide.4.text.text: The arm with a limit of 3 passes on attempt 2, and the loop ends there without using up the remaining attempts.

goal-loop.guide.5.text.text: The report states why it stopped. The arm with a limit of 1 stops at "达到尝试上限" ("attempt limit reached"), and the verdict is not passed.

goal-loop.conclusion.proves.0.text: Whether the loop continues is decided by this run's acceptance result and the limit on the task card; the events show each attempt's verdict and reason.

goal-loop.conclusion.proves.1.text: With a limit of 1 the loop stops after the first failure, and the report honestly says not passed.

goal-loop.conclusion.does_not_prove.0.text: The correction in attempt 2 is a fixed script; it does not show that a real model will necessarily correct it after reading the reason.

goal-loop.conclusion.does_not_prove.1.text: This lesson's limits and reasons are very simple; a real goal loop also needs budgets, timeouts, and give-up conditions, covered in {{lesson:goal-loops}}.

inputs.claim.help.text: Written into the summary of lesson.completion_claim. The acceptance check does not look at this sentence.

inputs.max_attempts.help.text: Takes effect only in the goal loop scenario, 1 to 3 attempts.

quiz.q1.prompt.text: The flow ran to the end but there is no tool result. Can you say the task is complete?

quiz.q1.a.text.text: Yes, the program has ended normally.

quiz.q1.a.feedback.text: "Ended normally" is only the run's terminal state, not an acceptance verdict; this lesson's "Claim only, no evidence" case also reached the end, yet was judged not passed.

quiz.q1.b.text.text: No, you also need an independent check and more evidence.

quiz.q1.b.feedback.text: Correct. The task card requires both successful tool evidence and the value condition to be met, and only after an independent check can you say it is complete.

quiz.q1.explanation.text: The run's terminal state and the acceptance verdict are two different things; without tool evidence it cannot pass.

quiz.three-dones.prompt.text: The "Claim only, no evidence" arm has finished: the terminal state is completed and the claimed answer is 42. Which statement is right?

quiz.three-dones.a.text.text: The flow ended, but there is no tool evidence, so acceptance failed

quiz.three-dones.a.feedback.text: Correct. The flow ending and the answer happening to be right cannot replace the computation evidence the task card requires.

quiz.three-dones.b.text.text: The answer is right, so the task is complete

quiz.three-dones.b.feedback.text: Not quite. The task card requires a basis in a local computation, and without a computation record that cannot be shown.

quiz.three-dones.c.text.text: The terminal state is completed, so acceptance passed

quiz.three-dones.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The terminal state only says the flow ran through; the acceptance verdict is decided by the evidence and the task card.

quiz.three-dones.explanation.text: The flow ending, the tool succeeding, and acceptance passing are three different things, to be judged separately.

quiz.q2.prompt.text: The executor's claim says "done, the answer is 42". Does it change the acceptance result?

quiz.q2.a.text.text: No; acceptance still rests on the cited tool evidence and the expected value.

quiz.q2.a.feedback.text: Correct. The claim is recorded, but the verdict is decided only by the evidence and the task card.

quiz.q2.b.text.text: Yes; claiming completion should be enough to pass.

quiz.q2.b.feedback.text: A claim is not evidence. If saying "done" were enough to pass, the acceptance check would be meaningless.

quiz.q2.explanation.text: Acceptance needs a fixed basis for judgment; a claim and its tone cannot replace evidence.

quiz.q3.prompt.text: The tool really returned 41 and the run had no exception. What verdict follows from the task card?

quiz.q3.a.text.text: Passed, because the tool was indeed called.

quiz.q3.a.feedback.text: Having called the tool satisfies only the condition that tool evidence exists; the value condition is not met, so it still cannot pass.

quiz.q3.b.text.text: Not passed, because the result does not match the goal of 42.

quiz.q3.b.feedback.text: Correct. Tool evidence exists, but 41 is not 42, so the value check fails.

quiz.q3.explanation.text: Having tool evidence is only one item; the value condition must be met too.

quiz.q4.prompt.text: The goal loop's limit is set to 1, and attempt 1 did not pass. What should happen next?

quiz.q4.a.text.text: Stop, and state in the report that the attempt limit was reached and acceptance failed.

quiz.q4.a.feedback.text: Correct. The limit is part of the task card; when it is reached, stop and say clearly why.

quiz.q4.b.text.text: Try again, since the reason is now known.

quiz.q4.b.feedback.text: Not quite. Retrying beyond the limit is the same as having no stop condition.

quiz.q4.c.text.text: Change the result to passed to avoid failing the task.

quiz.q4.c.feedback.text: Not quite. Reaching the limit decides only whether to stop; it does not change the acceptance verdict.

quiz.q4.explanation.text: The stop condition and the acceptance verdict are two different things: the former decides when to stop, the latter reports the result honestly.

check-hunt.prompt.text: Find the step where the tool evidence that acceptance rests on was produced.

check-hunt.explanation.text: It is the tool_result of add_numbers. Three report items, "工具成功返回" ("the tool returned successfully"), "证据中的值满足任务卡" ("the value in the evidence meets the task card"), and "声明与证据一致" ("the claim agrees with the evidence"), all read the result here. Neither the flow ending nor the executor's claim can replace this step; in the "Claim only, no evidence" case this step does not exist, so acceptance cannot pass.

check-points.prompt.text: Compare your own run with this lesson's source, and tick each item once you have done it.

check-points.item-1.text.text: I can state the goal, evidence, and failure conditions the task card specifies in this lesson.

check-points.item-2.text.text: I ran "Claim only, no evidence" or "Evidence present, wrong result" and saw the flow end while acceptance failed.

check-points.item-3.text.text: I ran "Claim and evidence disagree" and can point out which check blocked it.

check-points.item-4.text.text: I compared the reports for a goal loop limit of 3 and of 1, and can state the stop reason of each.

code_notes.input_scope.note.text: A task card field: limits the inputs that may be used; in this lesson only 19 and 23, with no external files or web pages.

code_notes.evidence.note.text: A task card field: which evidence acceptance looks at and what condition it must meet; in this lesson, the computation tool returned successfully and the result equals 42.

code_notes.failure.note.text: A task card field: when the tool fails, evidence is missing, or the value does not match, it must be clearly marked as not passed.

code_notes.stop.note.text: A task card field: when to stop. In the goal loop it is rewritten as "验收通过或尝试 N 次后停止" ("stop on acceptance or after N attempts").

code_notes.evidence_ref.note.text: A field in the completion claim whose value is the id of a tool call; verify uses it to look up the tool result recorded this run.

code_notes.next.note.text: A field of lesson.goal_check: the decision after this attempt; retry means try again, stop means stop.

code_notes.INPUT_MODEL.note.text: This lesson's input validation model: the scenario can only be one of the five presets, and the attempt limit only 1 to 3.

code_notes.completed.note.text: One of the run terminal states; it only says the program ran through normally, not that the task passed acceptance.
